extracted.intended_audience: students of political theory, constitutional designers, and the informed public interested in bicameral legislatures
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for judging the usefulness, composition, and function of an Upper House (second chamber) within a constitutional system, with particular reference to the British House of Lords and comparative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevents the rule of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of nobility prevents the rule of wealth--the religion of gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocracy restrains a society's simple admiration of money (wealth 'pur et simple') and the social dominance of newly-made rich men. Example: 'There is no country where a "poor devil of a millionaire is so ill off as in England"' — aristocracy keeps money 'kept down' by a different predominant authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserves manner and social STYLE
rubrics_metrics.description: Reverence for hereditary rank preserves manner, which is one of the fine arts and the STYLE of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manner (unconscious grace of life) should ideally belong to the aristocracy; it is compared to literary expression in written intercourse. This social skill is a physiological possession of the race but may be lacking in individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevents the idolatry of office
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy protects society from elevating petty officials into objects of worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where office is idolized (as on the Continent), petty officials obtain undue social prestige despite low pay or monotonous work. The aristocracy counteracts this by assigning prestige to great offices requiring mind rather than to minor places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provides durable social prestige and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereditary rank confers lasting respect and obedience from the populace, regardless of current wealth or solvency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An old lord commands deference even after ruin; this obedience awakens a sensation of submission in the 'coarse, dull, contracted multitude' and has social utility in maintaining order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second chamber as revising and suspending house
rubrics_metrics.description: The Upper House should function chiefly as a revising and suspending chamber, able to alter or temporarily reject bills rather than being co-equal with the Lower House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since the Lords' veto is often hypothetical ('We reject your Bill for this once or these twice...but if you keep on sending it up, at last we won't reject it'), the proper role is to revise detail and delay rather than to permanently block legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid co-equal bicameral deadlock
rubrics_metrics.description: Two co-ordinate Houses of distinct natures (both with equal authority) create the risk of deadlock and are a constitutional blemish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: American and Swiss systems may produce maximum impediment (dead-lock) because their Upper Houses are co-ordinate. The author argues that equality of veto power across Houses is not self-evidently expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of an available authority (escape-valve)
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be in every Constitution an available authority somewhere that can be 'come-at' to resolve persistent deadlock (e.g., Crown's power to create peers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability of the executive (or Crown) to create new members in the Upper House (or otherwise alter its composition) functions as a practical remedy to force a yielding and prevent paralysis, as in the Reform Act example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from social bribe and constituency pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: A good second chamber must be independent: free from constituency pressure and from being bought by social bribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Lords have no constituency to fear and are 'those who give social bribes, and not those who take them', they can form disinterested and cool judgments; the press and position-driven incentives that affect Commons members are less operative here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure to form judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the Upper House must have leisure and freedom from distracting occupations so they can devote time to careful revision and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers, having fewer distracting occupations, can 'bury themselves in' deliberation. Leisure is paired with independence and position to enable intellectual revision of legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical efficacy depends on active, capable membership
rubrics_metrics.description: An Upper House is only effective if it has a sufficient number of active, capable members who take part in ordinary business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A defect noted is that the Lords often have very few peers attending and speaking; 'perhaps ten peers, possibly only six'—the mass of the House may be 'nothing', making it ineffective in ordinary transaction of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition must suit deliberative functions (non-hereditary qualities matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The qualities that fit a man for marked eminence in a deliberative assembly are not hereditary and are not necessarily found in great landowners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic mismatch: dukes were locally great but 'as soon as the House met, Lord Thurlow became the greatest' because abilities for debate, rapid business, and speaking are not tied to descent; proxies and influence in Commons were used to compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper House useful as check on minor, technical, or interest-driven measures
rubrics_metrics.description: A revising chamber is valuable for controlling casual majorities in the Lower House on minor or technical matters which the nation does not attend to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower House majorities can be captured temporarily by specific interests (e.g., '200 "members for the railways"'), and an Upper House differently composed is likely not to be ruled by such interests and can restrain minor Parliamentary tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper House cannot be relied on to resist determined revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: A second chamber is not a true bulwark against revolution: it lacks force and cannot use the sword; when the nation and executive are resolved, a second chamber cannot arrest revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real deterrents are the executive and the army; the Lords' power is pacific and rests on deference rather than coercive capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper House as index of social stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence and retained power of a second chamber can serve as an index that revolution is unlikely; it signals lingering deference and social calm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: while old leaves linger on trees you know there has been little frost—similarly, a powerful House of Lords indicates little desperate discontent in the country.

rubrics_metrics.name: In federations, an Upper House embodies local feeling and equality symbolism
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal senate has the advantage of embodying a local (state) feeling; equality of representation in the Upper House symbolizes state identity and commands respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although equal representation (e.g., Delaware vs. New York) is not actually equal in power, the Senate's token of old independence preserves and commands deference in federations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two chambers may be harmful in colonies with too few able people
rubrics_metrics.description: In colonies or small polities a second assembly can be mischievous because it extracts the best men from the popular assembly and neutralizes them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Grey's colonial experience: second chambers in colonies denuded the lower house of best leaders, weakening popular assembly; thus a second chamber can strengthen democracy by isolating elite opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower House defects justify need for a revising chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the House of Commons lacks leisure, faces a distracting routine, handles excessive detail, and is subject to sudden combinations, a revising chamber is of great utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary business covers diverse and shifting matters (India, China, private bills) and the Commons does much legislative detail itself; committees and 'committee of the whole House' processes produce imperfect Acts—hence the value of a dedicated revising body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper House should have the position and authority to revise effectually
rubrics_metrics.description: An effective revising chamber must possess social position and institutional authority sufficient to influence and correct the Lower House's detailed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great offices with aristocratic associations (e.g., Treasury) give social prestige; an Under-Secretary of State may outrank a wealthier director in social terms, which helps the House's revising role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence must be real, not merely nominal
rubrics_metrics.description: The effectiveness of a second chamber depends on genuine independence of judgment rather than mere form or title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Lords' independence is tied to lack of constituency and lesser susceptibility to press and position inducements; but independence can be undermined by inactivity or by the executive's ability to alter composition.
